newsitem.title: USA: Tax limitation top Calif. challenge - survey.
newsitem.headline: Tax limitation top Calif. challenge - survey.

text.p: Taxpayer initiatives and tax-limitation measures are the biggest challenges facing California municipalities in the next decade, according to a survey released on Thursday.

Current tax limitations and taxpayer initiatives were each cited by a third of respondents in the survey as the top challenges for the next decade -- nearly triple the next concern, public safety costs, according to the survey.
These tax-related issues were among the top three issues for four of five respondents, compared with 63 percent who cited public safety costs, the survey said.

The survey of nearly 400 government officials in the state and public finance professionals was sponsored by MBIA Insurance Corp, a unit of MBIA Inc, and the Bond Buyer newspaper. The survey was released Thursday at a Bond Buyer public finance conference here.

"These findings suggest that municipal issuers will face increasing difficulties in financing their growing infrastructure needs," said John Pizzarelli, managing director of the western region of MBIA's public finance group. "You'll see more financings backed by sources other than property taxes, such as road tolls and lease payments through certificates of participation that fund education needs."

Institutional investors mentioned lease revenue and certificate of participation issuance as the area of public finance likely to show the most growth in the next five years, according to the MBIA poll.

The survey also found that the collapse of Orange County's investment pool has had wide-ranging effects on the state, with more than 60 percent of the local government respondents reporting their municipality has revised or created investment policies since the county filed for bankruptcy in late 1994.

About one-third of local government respondents said that in the last year their municipality had decreased the use of repurchase agreements and derivatives as well as the average life of their investment portfolios, the survey said.
Nearly half of issuers and government officials said Orange County's problems have raised their own financing costs, the survey found.

Among institutional investors, however, the impact of the Orange County bankruptcy appears to have waned. Nearly three- quarters reported in the survey that the county's restructuring efforts have had no effect on their appetite for municipal bonds issued within the state.

On the issue of disclosure, only 10 percent of respondents said the Securities and Exchange Commission has communicated well about new disclosure standards -- while 37 percent said the agency had done a poor job.

Only 43 percent said issuers understood their obligations to provide continuing disclosure to the market after their bonds are sold, the survey found. Eighty-seven percent of those with an opinion said improved disclosure would be positive for the market in the long term, according to the survey.

Twenty-six percent of respondents predicted 1997 new issue, long-term volume would range between $160 billion and $179 billion. More than 90 percent said the portion of new issuance backed by bond insurance would either increase or remain the same next year, the survey said.
